recipe: Wrap your async data mutation in `startTransition` to get automatic pending state management instead of manually toggling `isPending` with `useState`.
trigger_condition: You are handling an async operation (e.g., form submission) and need to manage its pending state.
evidence: In React 19, we're adding support for using async functions in transitions to handle pending states, errors, forms, and optimistic updates automatically.

recipe: Use `useActionState` to simplify form handling, as it returns a wrapped action, the last result, and pending state automatically.
trigger_condition: You are handling form submissions with async data mutations and want to avoid manually managing pending state and error handling.
evidence: To make the common cases easier for Actions, we've added a new hook called `useActionState`

recipe: Pass an async function directly to the `action` or `formAction` prop of `<form>`, `<input>`, or `<button>` elements to automatically submit forms with Actions.
trigger_condition: You need to handle form submissions that involve async data mutations.
evidence: We've added support for passing functions as the `action` and `formAction` props of `<form>`, `<input>`, and `<button>` elements to automatically submit forms with Actions

recipe: Use `useFormStatus` in design components to read the parent form's pending state without drilling props down.
trigger_condition: You are writing reusable design components (e.g., buttons) that need to know the status of the enclosing form.
evidence: to make the common case easier, we've added a new hook `useFormStatus`

recipe: Use `useOptimistic` to immediately render the final state while an async request is in progress, and let React automatically revert to the original value when the update finishes or errors.
trigger_condition: You need to show optimistic UI updates (e.g., displaying a new value before the server confirms it) during an async data mutation.
evidence: we're adding a new hook called `useOptimistic` to make this easier

recipe: Use the `use` API to read promises in render, letting React suspend until the promise resolves.
trigger_condition: You need to read a promise (e.g., a fetched resource) during component render.
evidence: In React 19 we're introducing a new API to read resources in render: `use`.

recipe: Use `use` instead of `useContext` when you need to read Context after an early return in a component.
trigger_condition: Your component has an early return before the point where you need to read a Context value.
evidence: You can also read context with `use`, allowing you to read Context conditionally such as after early returns

recipe: Do not pass a promise created in render to `use`; instead, pass a promise from a Suspense-compatible library or framework that supports caching.
trigger_condition: You are using the `use` API with a promise.

recipe: Unlike hooks, `use` can be called conditionally, so you can read resources only when needed without violating the rules of hooks.
trigger_condition: You need to read a resource (promise or context) only under certain conditions during render.
evidence: Unlike hooks, `use` can be called conditionally.

recipe: Use `prerender` from `react-dom/static` to generate static HTML that waits for all data to load before returning the stream, and send it via a streaming response.
trigger_condition: When you need static HTML generation in a streaming environment (Node.js Streams or Web Streams) that should wait for data to load.
evidence: Prerender APIs will wait for all data to load before returning the static HTML stream.

recipe: Pin to a specific React version or use the Canary release when building support for Server Components as a bundler or framework.
trigger_condition: When implementing a React Server Components bundler or framework, because the underlying APIs do not follow semver.
evidence: To support React Server Components as a bundler or framework, we recommend pinning to a specific React version, or using the Canary release.

recipe: Define Server Actions with the `"use server"` directive so Client Components can call async functions executed on the server.
trigger_condition: When you need Client Components to call async functions that run on the server.
evidence: When a Server Action is defined with the `"use server"` directive, your framework will automatically create a reference to the server function, and pass that reference to the Client Component.

recipe: Access `ref` as a prop in function components instead of wrapping with `forwardRef`.
trigger_condition: When writing new function components that need to accept a ref.

recipe: Render `<Context>` directly as a provider instead of using `<Context.Provider>`.
trigger_condition: When creating new Context providers in React 19.
evidence: In React 19, you can render `<Context>` as a provider instead of `<Context.Provider>`:

recipe: Return a cleanup function from `ref` callbacks to run cleanup logic when the component unmounts.
trigger_condition: When you need to clean up resources associated with a ref when the component unmounts.
evidence: When the component unmounts, React will call the cleanup function returned from the `ref` callback.

recipe: Use explicit returns (braces) in ref callbacks instead of implicit returns, since returning anything other than a cleanup function will now be rejected by TypeScript.
trigger_condition: When a ref callback implicitly returns a value (e.g., `ref={current => (instance = current)}`) and TypeScript complains after upgrading to React 19.
evidence: Due to the introduction of ref cleanup functions, returning anything else from a `ref` callback will now be rejected by TypeScript. The fix is usually to stop using implicit returns

recipe: Render `<title>`, `<link>`, and `<meta>` tags directly in your components; React will automatically hoist them to the `<head>` section of the document.
trigger_condition: When you need to set document metadata from a component that is not rendering the `<head>`.
evidence: When React renders this component, it will see the `<title>` `<link>` and `<meta>` tags, and automatically hoist them to the `<head>` section of document.

recipe: When debugging hydration mismatches, check for server/client branching, variable input such as `Date.now()` or `Math.random()`, locale-dependent date formatting, external changing data without a snapshot, or invalid HTML tag nesting.
trigger_condition: When you encounter a hydration error where server-rendered HTML doesn't match client rendering.
evidence: Variable input such as `Date.now()` or `Math.random()` which changes each time it's called.

recipe: Use the `precedence` attribute on `<link>` elements to control stylesheet insertion order in the DOM; React will ensure external stylesheets are loaded before revealing content that depends on them.
trigger_condition: When you need to manage the loading order of stylesheets that affect your component's rendering.
evidence: If you tell React the `precedence` of your stylesheet it will manage the insertion order of the stylesheet in the DOM and ensure that the stylesheet (if external) is loaded before revealing content that depends on those style rules.

recipe: Render `<script async>` tags inside the components that actually depend on them rather than manually managing script relocation and deduplication.
trigger_condition: When you need to load a third-party script used by a specific component deep in your component tree.
evidence: In React 19 we've included better support for async scripts by allowing you to render them anywhere in your component tree, inside the components that actually depend on the script, without having to manage relocating and deduplicating script instances.

recipe: Use `prefetchDNS`, `preconnect`, `preload`, and `preinit` from `react-dom` to proactively load resources before they are needed, either for initial page loads or anticipated client-side navigations.
trigger_condition: When you want to optimize initial page loads or client-side updates by preloading resources that will be needed soon.
evidence: React 19 includes a number of new APIs for loading and preloading Browser resources to make it as easy as possible to build great experiences that aren't held back by inefficient resource loading.

recipe: Use the `onCaughtError`, `onUncaughtError`, and `onRecoverableError` root options to handle React errors with a single consolidated log instead of the previous behavior of duplicate error logging.
trigger_condition: When you need to handle errors in your React application and want fine-grained control over caught, uncaught, and recoverable errors.
evidence: we've added two new root options to complement `onRecoverableError`: - `onCaughtError`: called when React catches an error in an Error Boundary. - `onUncaughtError`: called when an error is thrown and not caught by an Error Boundary.

recipe: Be aware that unexpected tags in `<head>` and `<body>` inserted by third-party scripts or browser extensions are skipped during hydration, avoiding mismatch errors.
trigger_condition: When your app uses third-party scripts or browser extensions that modify the DOM during the hydration process.
evidence: In React 19, unexpected tags in the `<head>` and `<body>` will be skipped over, avoiding the mismatch errors.
